common_name: Rockapulco Red Impatiens (Fully Double Rose-Bud Impatiens)

planting.note: Plant purchased transplants after all frost danger has passed in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full shade. Rockapulco is a Proven Winners series bred for fully double, rose-bud-like flowers and improved heat and humidity tolerance compared to older double impatiens strains.

directions: Plant in partial to full shade in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Rockapulco Red is a Proven Winners impatiens bred for fully double, ruffled, rose-like red blooms that resemble small roses more than a typical five-petaled impatiens flower, held over a compact, mounding plant that continues flowering non-stop from spring through frost in deep shade where few other bedding annuals bloom well at all. Like other Impatiens walleriana selections it remains susceptible to impatiens downy mildew, the fungal disease that has caused serious losses in impatiens plantings across North America since 2011; provide good air circulation, avoid overhead watering, and consider New Guinea impatiens or SunPatiens in areas with a known history of the disease. Deadheading is not required since spent blooms drop cleanly on their own, and consistent moisture keeps the display at its best through summer heat.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Annual Flowers for Shade

common_name: SuperCal Neon Rose Petchoa (Petunia-Calibrachoa Intergeneric Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant purchased transplants after all frost danger has passed in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Petchoa is a naturally occurring intergeneric hybrid between petunia and calibrachoa, propagated only from cuttings, and combines petunia-size blooms with calibrachoa's tougher, more weather-resistant constitution.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun in a container, hanging basket, or bed. SuperCal Neon Rose is a Petchoa — a naturally occurring intergeneric cross between petunia and calibrachoa (million bells) — that combines the larger, showier flower size of petunia with the smaller leaf, tougher constitution, and better rain and heat tolerance of calibrachoa, producing masses of vivid neon-pink, petunia-shaped flowers on a mounding, trailing plant that holds up better through summer storms than a standard petunia. Like calibrachoa, it is largely self-cleaning and needs no deadheading to keep flowering heavily. Feed regularly through the season, since the vigorous, continuous bloom draws heavily on the plant's reserves, and trim back by up to a third in mid-summer if growth becomes leggy to encourage fresh, dense regrowth and renewed flowering.

planting.note: Plant purchased transplants or start seed indoors well ahead of last frost, since begonia seed is extremely fine and slow to reach transplant size; set out after frost danger has passed in moist, well-drained, fertile soil, in anything from full shade to full sun.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in anywhere from full shade to full sun, provided soil moisture stays consistent; Surefire Red is a Proven Winners Begonia benariensis selection bred for unusual versatility across light levels — unlike traditional wax begonias, which are strictly shade to part-shade plants, Surefire performs well in full sun as readily as in shade, and it also carries strong resistance to the bacterial and fungal diseases that can trouble begonia plantings in hot, humid conditions. It produces a continuous, self-cleaning display of bright red flowers over glossy, deep-green foliage from spring through frost, with no deadheading required. This light-level flexibility makes it a useful choice for beds that get a mix of sun and shade through the day, where a strictly shade-only or sun-only begonia would perform unevenly. Water regularly through hot weather and feed lightly through the season for the best continuous bloom.
sources: university extension AAS trial garden notes

common_name: Megawatt Pink Bronze Leaf Begonia (Oversized Non-Stop Begonia)
scientific_name: Begonia interspecific hybrid 'Megawatt Pink Bronze Leaf'

planting.note: Plant purchased transplants after all frost danger has passed in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; Megawatt is an interspecific begonia bred for an unusually large plant size and heavy, continuous bloom through summer heat and dry spells.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; Megawatt Pink Bronze Leaf is a large-scale interspecific begonia bred to dwarf standard wax and even many landscape begonias, forming a substantial, well-branched mound topped with an unusually heavy, non-stop show of clear pink flowers set off by bronze-tinted foliage. It tolerates more heat, sun, and drought than traditional shade begonias once established, and its bold size and continuous bloom make single plants effective as focal points in large containers or landscape beds rather than needing to be massed for impact. It is self-cleaning and needs no deadheading. Water deeply during dry spells, especially in a full-sun position, and feed regularly through the growing season to sustain its vigorous size and heavy flower production.

common_name: Akila Purple Osteospermum (Self-Branching Seed African Daisy)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant 2-4 weeks before last frost as plants tolerate light frost. Akila is a seed-grown osteospermum series bred to branch and flower heavily on its own without pinching, unlike older seed strains that needed more grooming to fill out.

directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in well-drained germination mix, then transplant into full sun in well-drained soil once the worst frost risk has passed, since young plants tolerate light frost. Akila Purple is a seed-grown African daisy bred to branch and flower heavily right out of the pack without the pinching or grooming that older seed-raised osteospermum varieties needed to fill out into a full, floriferous plant, giving growers a vegetative-quality, uniform show from seed. The rich purple, daisy-form flowers with dark centers open on a compact, well-branched mound that performs best in the cooler shoulder seasons and slows during peak summer heat, similar to other osteospermums. Deadhead spent flowers to keep the display tidy and encourage continued bloom; in zone 9-11 gardens it can persist as a short-lived perennial, especially with a light summer trim to keep it from stretching in the heat.
sources: PanAmerican Seed — Akila Osteospermum series documentation

common_name: Techno Heat White Lobelia (Heat-Tolerant Trailing Lobelia)

planting.note: Start the very fine seed indoors well ahead of the last frost, pressing it onto the surface since it needs light to germinate. Techno Heat is bred to keep flowering through summer heat rather than shutting down the way standard trailing lobelia typically does once temperatures climb.

directions: Start the very fine seed indoors, pressing it onto the surface of moist mix without covering since it needs light to germinate; transplant after frost danger has passed into moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun. Techno Heat White is a trailing lobelia bred specifically to resist the summer heat dieback that causes most Lobelia erinus varieties to stop blooming and go into decline once temperatures climb into the 80s and 90s, extending its display of small, pure-white flowers over cascading, fine-textured foliage well into the hot part of the growing season. It works well in hanging baskets, window boxes, and container edges. Keep soil consistently moist, since lobelia has a shallow root system that dries out quickly in containers, and provide afternoon shade in the hottest climates to further extend bloom. A light midseason shearing encourages a fresh flush of flowers if the plant thins out.
sources: Syngenta Flowers — Techno Lobelia series documentation

common_name: Skyscraper Orange Salvia (Tall Well-Branched Pollinator Salvia)

planting.note: Plant purchased transplants after the last frost into well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Skyscraper Orange is a tall, tender perennial salvia grown as a warm-season annual outside its hardiness range, valued for large tubular flowers held on strong, self-branching upright stems.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Skyscraper Orange is a tall, sturdy, well-branched salvia bred for a strong upright habit that holds large, vivid orange tubular flowers on tall spikes without flopping, making it a good back-of-border choice or a bold single accent in a large container. The oversized flowers and long bloom season from summer through frost make it a magnet for hummingbirds and larger pollinators, which can reach deep into the tubular blooms that smaller flowers can't offer. It performs as a tender perennial in zones 8-10, where it may return from the roots after a mild winter, and as a warm-season annual farther north. Deadhead spent spikes to encourage continued branching and bloom, and pinch young plants once to promote a fuller, sturdier base before the tall flowering stems take over.

common_name: Soiree Kawaii Red Shades Vinca (Micro-Bloom Disease-Resistant Vinca)

planting.note: Start indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost, or plant purchased transplants; set out only when nights are consistently above 55F. Soiree Kawaii is bred with improved resistance to Phytophthora, the soilborne rot that is the most common cause of vinca bedding failures in hot, wet conditions.

directions: Transplant into well-drained soil in full sun only after nights are reliably warm, since cold, wet soil stalls and yellows young vinca plants. Soiree Kawaii Red Shades is a compact annual vinca bred for a profusion of small, closely spaced deep-red flowers in a tidy mounding habit, along with meaningfully improved resistance to Phytophthora root and stem rot, the fungal disease most responsible for sudden vinca collapse in the humid, rain-prone conditions of a Gulf South summer. Like other vinca it is naturally heat- and drought-tolerant and self-cleaning, needing no deadheading to keep flowering non-stop through the hottest part of the season, and it generally outperforms impatiens and other shade annuals in a full-sun bed once truly warm weather sets in. Avoid overwatering and improve soil drainage before planting, since even disease-resistant vinca still performs poorly in soggy soil.
sources: Suntory Flowers — Soiree Vinca series documentation

common_name: Supertunia Bordeaux Petunia (Wine-Purple Veined Spreading Petunia)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Supertunia Bordeaux is a vigorous mounding-to-trailing petunia bred for deep wine-purple flowers with fine darker veining, well suited to large containers, hanging baskets, and landscape beds.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, giving it room to spread. Supertunia Bordeaux produces a vigorous mounding, trailing plant smothered in rich wine-purple flowers finely traced with darker veining, largely self-cleaning so it needs very little deadheading to keep flowering heavily from spring through frost. Its vigorous but somewhat more restrained spread than the largest Supertunia selections makes it a versatile choice for mixed containers, hanging baskets, and landscape mass plantings alike. Feed regularly to sustain the continuous bloom, and shear the plant back by a third if it becomes leggy in the heat of summer to encourage fresh, dense regrowth and a renewed flush of flowers.

common_name: Alumia Vanilla Cream Marigold (Large Anemone-Type Soft Yellow Marigold)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost, or direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed; Alumia Vanilla Cream is a vigorous, early-flowering French marigold bred for large, densely double, anemone-form flowers in a soft, unusual lemon-cream color.

directions: Direct sow after the last frost, or transplant started seedlings, into well-drained soil in full sun. Alumia Vanilla Cream is a French marigold bred for unusually large, fully double, anemone-form flowers in a soft, creamy lemon-yellow that stands apart from the typical bright orange and gold of most marigolds, opening early and continuing vigorously through the season on a well-branched, uniform plant. Its large flower size and gentle color make it useful as a softer accent in mixed plantings that would clash with brighter marigold tones. Marigolds tolerate poor, lean soil and bloom best without heavy fertilizer, which favors foliage over flowers; deadhead spent blooms to keep the display tidy and encourage continued flowering, and water at the base rather than overhead to help avoid the powdery mildew and botrytis that can affect dense marigold plantings in humid weather.
sources: Syngenta Flowers — Alumia Marigold series documentation
